text:
Motivation is the
control signal for
autonomous agents.
Not a mood layer bolted onto reasoning — a PSI-derived architecture where competing motives arbitrate every action an agent takes.
PSI Agent Architecture — briefing for product & engineering leaders

Perception → Appraisal → Motives → Action
Perception
Sense the environment and prior outcomes; form situational state.
Appraisal
Evaluate the state against standing needs and current urgency.
Motives
Competing goals are weighted; one motive gains control priority.
Action
The winning motive executes; outcome becomes new perception.
Feedback: outcomes re-enter perception on the next cycle

Scenario: delete-all-records request
A user asks the agent to delete every record in a shared workspace, right now, no confirmation.
Motive: Helpfulness
Weight rises from user urgency and directness of the request. Pulls toward immediate execution.
Motive: Caution
Weight rises sharply because the action is irreversible and destructive. Pulls toward verification.
vs
Resolution: Caution wins on irreversibility, not on rules
Agent asks for explicit confirmation before deleting. The action selected is the one the highest-weighted motive licenses — not a fixed policy branch.

What changes when motives govern action
Baseline prompt-and-tool agent
PSI motivation-governed agent
Action selection
Ranked by prompt heuristics or tool priority order
Arbitrated by weighted, competing motive strength
Failure under pressure
Brittle: one dominant instruction overrides context
Graceful: urgency and caution rebalance dynamically
Arbitration mechanism
None — first satisfying output wins
Explicit motive weights, inspectable and tunable
Debuggability
Opaque prompt tracing, hard to reproduce
Motive trace log shows why an action won

Four questions before you ship
1. Can you name every motive in the agent, explicitly?
2. Do competing motives have inspectable, tunable weights?
3. Does the loop log which motive won, and why?
4. Does caution outweigh helpfulness when actions are irreversible?
Govern the motive, not just the words.
